title: Bouncing ball

reference.basis: plain white sheet on wall taken as A4 standard

slow_motion.evidence: no on-screen text or narration indicates slow motion

subjects.description: small glossy red spherical ball falling and bouncing

observation.what_happens: A red ball starts in mid-air left of a paper on the wall and falls toward the brown floor while drifting right. It bounces repeatedly on the floor and ends resting on the floor on the right side.

calibration.note: white paper = 0.297 m (plain white sheet on wall taken as A4 standard) spans 143 px in SAM's mask

given: scale: white paper = 0.297 m (plain white sheet on wall taken as A4 standard) spans 143 px in SAM's mask, known to ±6%
reasoning: x drifts right almost steadily while y shows repeated asymmetric arcs falling fast and rising lower, classic gravity bounces decaying from ~0.68m to ~0.43m to ~0.26m implying e~0.78. Candidates go from textbook vacuum bounce to quadratic air drag to linear drag with floor friction to test if air or sideways scrub improves prediction of the later settling bounces.

law.title: Gravity plus bouncy floor
law.summary: The ball falls under gravity and bounces off the floor keeping its bounce height ratio the same.

params.name: e
params.meaning: vertical restitution, outgoing over incoming speed

fitted.title: Gravity plus bouncy floor
fitted.summary: The ball falls under gravity and bounces off the floor keeping its bounce height ratio the same.

params.name: e
params.meaning: vertical restitution, outgoing over incoming speed

candidates.ifItWins: Flight is vacuum ballistic and bounces lose energy only in the vertical direction.

law.title: Air drag plus bouncy floor
law.summary: Like gravity plus bounce but air pushes back harder the faster the ball goes.

params.name: k
params.meaning: quadratic air drag per mass, force = m*k*v^2

fitted.title: Air drag plus bouncy floor
fitted.summary: Like gravity plus bounce but air pushes back harder the faster the ball goes.

params.name: k
params.meaning: quadratic air drag per mass, force = m*k*v^2

candidates.ifItWins: Air slows the ball with force growing as speed squared plus a bouncy floor loss.

law.title: Textbook projectile (no air)
law.summary: Moves at constant horizontal speed while gravity pulls it down at a constant rate.

fitted.title: Textbook projectile (no air)
fitted.summary: Moves at constant horizontal speed while gravity pulls it down at a constant rate.

law.title: Viscous air plus grippy bounce
law.summary: The ball feels syrup-like air drag and the floor steals a little sideways speed on every bounce.

params.name: f
params.meaning: horizontal speed kept after bounce, friction loss

fitted.title: Viscous air plus grippy bounce
fitted.summary: The ball feels syrup-like air drag and the floor steals a little sideways speed on every bounce.

params.name: f
params.meaning: horizontal speed kept after bounce, friction loss

candidates.ifItWins: Flight has gentle viscous air drag and each bounce scrubs both vertical and horizontal speed.

caveats: Paper scale is known only to a few percent, so all heights shift together.
Sideways misses clump in long stretches, so horizontal motion is less trusted.
critique.finding: The ball is pulled down with g = {g} and bounces back keeping {e} of its fall speed. It captures up-down well but only partly captures the sideways drift.
critique.headline: Bouncing ball falls freely and rebounds on floor
critique.why_it_won: It adds a bouncy floor that follows every rebound while the plain projectile flies through the floor, and added air drag changes nothing.

headline: Bouncing ball falls freely and rebounds on floor
finding: The ball is pulled down with g = 9.43 ± 0.57 m/s² and bounces back keeping 0.79865 ± 0.00040 of its fall speed. It captures up-down well but only partly captures the sideways drift.

eyeball.law_in_words: vertical motion is constant-acceleration free fall y(t)=y0+v0*t-0.5*g*t^2, with scale from 0.297 m paper, fall time to first impact gives g, and at floor y=floor_y vertical velocity reverses with outgoing speed = e times incoming speed
